name: Burn Blue
lede: Burn Blue is a pale, slightly greyed blue-grey from the Ridgway and ISCC-NBS dictionaries, closer to a bluish white than to any strong blue.

sections.title: A 1912 plate, carried forward
sections.body:
Ridgway's 1912 color nomenclature lists it at plate XXXIV, hue 47'', with hex #B0BACB [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary of color repeats the same plate when the ISCC-NBS committee cited it in 1955, placing it in block 184 among the "very pale blue" names, 6.0 units from that category's center [1]. The Munsell renotation gives it as 5.4PB 7.5/2.9, a notation of low chroma that confirms how little blue is left in it once lightened this far [1].

Two near neighbors in the library sit within four units: [[pale-neropalin-blue|Pale Neropalin Blue]], 3.0 units away, and [[sky-grey|Sky Grey]], 3.9 units away, both slightly cooler and a touch lighter [1]. The name's own origin is not explained in the sources consulted here, and is undocumented [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A color within six units of Burn Blue covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 268 of 23,781 paintings, about 1.1 per cent, as photographed [2]. Its earliest appearance in the archive is a 1401 *Madonna and Child* by Lorenzo di Niccolò, where it covers only six per cent of the canvas [2]. It peaks in paintings from the 1510s, and Pierre Puvis de Chavannes and Alonso Cano use it far more than the archive average, each more than fourteen times the base rate [2]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not a pigment identification [2].
